text:
# Narration script: Sounding walkthrough (4:01)

Read at a relaxed pace. Each block's time window matches the video exactly, and the word counts are sized for a
calm speaking speed.

**Recording tips**
- Record in one go, or one block at a time. Pause for about 2 seconds between blocks.
- If you stumble, pause, then say the sentence again from the start. I'll keep the clean take.
- Don't rush to fit the times. If a block runs long, I hold the video on that screen a little longer, so nothing gets cut.
- Speak as if you're showing a colleague your screen. Sentences like "I did this because…" are the ones reviewers want.

---

### 1 · 0:00 – 0:10 · Title card
Hi, I'm Hamza. This is Sounding, my version of Fathom: an AI notetaker that turns a meeting recording into a transcript, notes, action items and clips.

### 2 · 0:10 – 0:14 · Login page
The live link works for anyone. Reviewers get in with one click.

### 3 · 0:14 – 0:29 · My calls
This is the meetings list. It's seeded with real recorded meetings, and everything you see here was generated by the pipeline: the titles, the meeting types, the one-line summaries, who spoke and how many action items are still open.

### 4 · 0:29 – 0:43 · The 8-person meeting, speakers
I started with the hardest case: an hour-long meeting with eight people. My first speaker model could only tell four voices apart, so I tested it against human labels and added a second pass that clusters voices. It now separates seven speakers, with far fewer mix-ups.

### 5 · 0:43 – 0:54 · Playback and transcript
When you press play, the transcript follows along with the recording. Clicking any line jumps straight to that moment, so you never have to scrub through an hour.

### 6 · 0:54 – 1:03 · Notes with timestamps
The notes are grouped into sections, and every point links back to where it was said. If the model cites a time that doesn't exist, I throw it away.

### 7 · 1:03 – 1:14 · Templates and action items
Changing the template rewrites the notes for that kind of meeting, like a sales call. Action items keep who said them and when, and you can assign each one to a teammate.

### 8 · 1:14 – 1:27 · Ask this meeting
You can also just ask the meeting a question. Here I'm asking what they decided about collecting more data. The answer comes back with timestamps, and each one takes you to the exact point in the call.

### 9 · 1:27 – 1:46 · Highlight and clip
The highlight button saves the last twenty seconds and the next ten, because by the time you think "that was important", the moment has already passed. You can also clip any range from the transcript. Then you can share just that clip with someone who wasn't on the call.

### 10 · 1:46 – 2:01 · Opening the clip logged out
To show it really works, I log out completely and open the link. The clip plays with its own transcript, and nothing else from the meeting is exposed.

### 11 · 2:01 – 2:21 · Search and Ask across meetings
Back in, search runs across every transcript and every set of notes, and results open right at the matching moment. Ask Sounding does the same thing across all your calls. It pulls the relevant parts from each meeting and answers with links to where each point came from.

### 12 · 2:21 – 2:36 · Trackers
Trackers watch for topics across every call. Keyword trackers look for exact words, and AI trackers look for meaning. So a deadline tracker catches "we need this by Friday" even though nobody said the word deadline.

### 13 · 2:36 – 2:47 · Coaching
Coaching shows talk time, questions and long monologues for each person. Scorecards grade each call against the criteria set for that type of meeting.

### 14 · 2:47 – 3:04 · Playlists, companies and sharing
Playlists collect clips from different meetings, and play all runs them back to back, which is handy for onboarding. Companies are grouped automatically from attendee emails. Every meeting can be private, shared with a team or shared with the whole organisation.
